feedback: If a learner recites decade names (7 → 10, 20, 30) and drops the 7: on the hundred square move straight DOWN the column from 7 to show 7, 17, 27 keep the ones digit; name aloud what stays (the 7) and what changes (the tens).

If the ones digit drifts (7, 17, 28, 38): do NOT reteach counting — highlight that the ones column stays the same, using place-value arrow cards or adding one ten-rod each time so the +10-only structure is felt.

If a learner stalls at the hundred boundary (fine to 97, then stuck or says 100, 110): extend the square past 100 and rehearse just the 97 → 107 → 117 bridge, pointing out the ones digit (7) still stays while the tens roll from 9 to 0 and a new hundred appears. Saying 100 means the ones digit has changed, so revisit what stays the same and give more practice crossing 100.

If a learner says +10 means 'add a 0' (27 → 270): compare 27+10 on the grid with the actual answer 37. Show that adding a 0 multiplies by ten, so it never gives +10, even for round numbers (20 with a 0 added is 200, but 20+10 = 30).
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting ten never touches the ones digit; it is the same single downward (or upward) step on the hundred square whatever number you start from. '+10' is not 'add a zero' — it is 'one row down'.
learnerActions: Start on a non-multiple, e.g. 27, on a hundred square.
Make a +10 move by dropping straight DOWN one row: 27 → 37 → 47 → 57, saying each number aloud.
Each step of this 27 → 57 run, point to the ones digit (the 7) and say 'the ones stay the same'; point to the tens digit and say 'the tens go up by one' (true while you stay inside a hundred).
Reverse it: make −10 moves by going straight UP one row: 83 → 73 → 63 → 53, saying what stays (the ones) and what changes (the tens).
Watch for drifting sideways — keep the move strictly vertical so you stay in the same ones-digit column.
activities.title: Down a column, ones frozen — the +10/−10 move on the hundred square

feedback: If a learner changes the ones to make +10, point out the ones pile should not have been touched and rebuild it.
Connect the blocks back to the digits: the number of ten-rods is the tens digit, the ones pile is the ones digit.
activities.intendedInsight: Physically, +10 is just one extra ten-rod; the ones stay as they are. This is the concrete reason the ones digit never changes.
learnerActions: Build a two-digit number with base-ten blocks, e.g. 23 as two ten-rods and three ones.
To add 10, bring in ONE more ten-rod and leave the ones pile untouched; read the new number (33).
To subtract 10, take one ten-rod away and leave the ones pile untouched; read the new number.
Say the rule as you go: 'one more ten, the ones don't change'.
Link each action to its numeral and, if available, to the hundred-square move.
activities.title: Concrete why: add a ten-rod with base-ten blocks

feedback: If a learner finds 10 more only by counting on in ones, encourage the direct 'one row down' move instead.
When a learner spots the wrong digit, ask them to correct it and state the rule.
Recognising a wrong sequence is a check; it does not by itself show the learner can produce a correct one, so also ask the learner to generate their own sequences aloud.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent +10/−10 from any starting number, with the ability to notice when the ones digit has wrongly moved.
learnerActions: Answer quick questions: 'What is 10 more than 47?' and 'What is 10 less than 47?'
Fill in a tens sequence from a non-multiple, e.g. 4, 14, __, __, 44.
Look at a wrong sequence (e.g. 7, 17, 28, 38) and say which digit changed that shouldn't have.
Count aloud forwards from a non-multiple and backwards from a two-digit number, stating each step is +10 or −10.
activities.title: Say-it and spot-the-slip practice

feedback: Accept explanations like 'you add one more ten, so the ones don't move'.
For ten more than 96, let the learner use the extended grid to see 96 → 106: point out that the ones digit (6) still does not move, while the tens roll from 9 to 0 and a new hundred appears.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to articulate that each step adds or removes one ten — so the ones digit always stays the same while the tens digit changes by one, rolling over into a new hundred at a boundary like 96 → 106 where the ones (6) still does not move — shows place-value reasoning rather than just the chant.
learnerActions: Count in tens from a non-multiple, then answer: 'What stays the same each time, and what changes?'
Answer in your own words why the ones digit stays the same each time and what happens to the tens.
Try harder prompts: ten less than 43 (33); ten more than 96 (106, crossing 100).
activities.title: Explain the pattern out loud
